en: You can ask the platform to fix the way it informs and make visible what matters, to show what it actually displayed and to make up for what you lost through the lack of clarity. The failure can be treated as a defect in the quality of information or as an abusive practice. It can even lead to the invalidity of clauses that go against what you had reason to expect.

The request starts with the records, which must be preserved and shown, and it can include an expert examination on defined points. You can also ask for a check, based on the minimum clarity the platform owes, of whether the change or the penalty was legitimate. If the platform does not produce the records only it had, there may be presumptions against it, which make certain facts count in your favor.

The request here is that the burden of proof be shared according to who has access to the evidence. Depending on the case, there may also be presumptions in your favor, which make certain facts count as true until proven otherwise, and a stronger duty on the platform to cooperate with the evidence.

The ad binds, so you can ask for the offer to be corrected and honored, for what you lost to be made good and for the misleading communication to stop. In some cases, you can ask for sales strategies that do not match what is really delivered to be struck down. The law may treat this as misleading or abusive advertising, or as an offer that binds whoever made it.

The central request is that consumer law keep applying. In practice, this can mean a limited examination of the records that protects trade secrets, and a check on the equivalence of what you bought. It can also mean that the company respects its duties of adequacy, transparency and restoration. And if the game shuts down, that the exit comes, as far as possible, with a transition, preservation or transfer of what you had inside.

The first request is that the problem be treated as an issue of the environment, and not as carelessness on your part. If this dependence on the platform's signals is shown, stronger duties to inform, advertise clearly and provide evidence may apply. Depending on the facts, the practice may be seen as abusive, as insufficient information or as deception through ambiguity or omission. Together with other elements, this can even change who has to prove what.
